content.text: There is no single best software track, and your first choice doesn't lock you in. Most of the daily work is shared across tracks, so the cheapest way to choose is to learn the common basics, try two or three tracks with small projects, then commit to one roadmap. Switching later is normal, and it costs less than people fear when you move to a neighboring track.

A student spends three months reading "best track" threads and asking every group chat which role has the most jobs. He picks AI because it's the loudest, and two months later he's stuck: he enjoyed the Python but hates the statistics and the data cleaning. He decides programming isn't for him and stops. What he needed wasn't a better answer to "which track". He needed two weekends of trying a few tracks, and the knowledge that the Python, Git and debugging he'd already learned carry over to every one of them.
The common misconception

The belief is that one track is objectively the best, and that the choice you make at the start decides your whole career. It's easy to see where it comes from. Online roadmaps are drawn per track, as if they never meet. Job ads ask for years of one specific framework. And when you've studied for months, switching feels like throwing that time away.

The reality is gentler. The tracks share most of their foundations, and real jobs blur the lines: in Stack Overflow's 2025 Developer Survey, "full-stack developer" was the role respondents picked most often, ahead of back-end. Plenty of engineers move between neighboring tracks during their careers. The right track is the one whose daily work you can stand on a bad day, and you only find that out by trying it.
What each track really does all day

Most of the day in every track is the same work. O*NET, the occupation database built for the U.S. Department of Labor, describes software developers analyzing user needs, modifying existing software to fix errors and improve performance, and conferring with other engineers about the design. The tracks differ in what that work touches:

rows.text: APIs, databases, business rules, performance and failures you can't see
You like logic, data and systems that must not break
Screens, layout, accessibility, browser quirks and speed
You care how things look and feel to a real user
A feature from the database to the button, at moderate depth on each side
You like owning a whole feature
Apps on small screens, offline use, device APIs and store releases
You like a product people hold in their hand
Pipelines, infrastructure as code, monitoring and alerts
You like automation and keeping things running
Risk assessments, monitoring, testing defenses, writing policies
You like thinking like an attacker, legally
Cleaning, querying and modeling data, dashboards, pipelines
You like finding the answer hidden in numbers
Building with models: data, evaluation, prompts, serving

content.text: The stages from your first try to senior
Durations assume about 10 hours a week; at 20 hours, expect roughly half. The later stages happen on the job and are measured in years of real work, so no fixed number fits them.

items.title: Stage 1: Learn the basics every track shares

content.text: Roughly 7–14 months at 10 hours a week.
Learn
one language, Git, data structures, and how operating systems and networks work, as laid out in Where to Start in Software.
Postpone
the choice itself: these basics are the same for every track.
Build
a command-line program in Git with a README.
You're ready
when you can build a small program on your own and you're curious what to build next.

items.title: Stage 2: Try two or three tracks with taster projects

content.text: About 1–2 months at 10 hours a week.
Learn

just enough of each track for one small project: a tiny API for backend, a page with a form for frontend, a one-screen app for mobile, a container with a CI pipeline for DevOps, a legal practice lab for security, or an analysis of a public dataset for data.
Postpone
paid courses, certifications and deep framework study.
Build
two or three tasters, a weekend or two each.
You're ready
when one of them kept you going after it was "done". Note which part you enjoyed: the logic, the visuals, the data or the infrastructure.

items.title: Stage 3: Commit to one track and follow its roadmap

content.text: Roughly 6–12 months at 10 hours a week to your first complete project.
Learn
your track's roadmap stage by stage and ignore the hype around the others for now.
Postpone
the second track.
Build
one real project in that track from start to deployment.
You're ready
when you can build and ship a small project in the track without a step-by-step guide.

items.title: Stage 4: Go deep, then a little wide

content.text: Your first years on the job.
Learn
depth in your track, plus enough of its neighbors to work across the boundary: a backend developer learns how the frontend calls the API and how the service is deployed.
Postpone
chasing every new framework.
Build
a feature that crosses a boundary, such as an endpoint and the screen that uses it.
You're ready
when you own tasks end to end and others come to you with questions.

items.title: Stage 5: As a senior, deepen or switch on purpose

content.text: Learn

what seniors own in your track: design decisions, reliability and mentoring. Switch when your interest has moved for months, not days, and move to a neighbor that reuses your skills, such as backend to DevOps or data engineering, frontend to mobile, or QA automation to backend.
Postpone
switching in the hard middle of a stage, when every track looks greener.
Build
a bridge project in the new track that uses what you already know.
You're ready
when the new track's daily work holds your interest as the old one once did.
Books for each stage

rows.text: Code: The Hidden Language of Computer Hardware and Software

content.text: None of these teaches a framework, which is why they age slowly. The Pragmatic Programmer's advice is language-neutral and holds up. The Guidebook describes career levels at tech companies and startups, mostly in the US and Europe, so treat its titles and promotion steps as one example; ladders at your company may differ. Each track's own roadmap lists the technical books for that track.
Common mistakes

items.text: picking the loudest track this year, or the one a friend picked, without trying it.
reading comparisons for months when two weekends of tasters would answer the question.
every track has a hard middle, and jumping then resets you to the easy start of another one.
the basics, Git, debugging and your way of working all move with you.

content.text: Ask what you can stand on a bad day, not what looks good on a good one: a layout that breaks in one browser, a pipeline that fails at night, a dataset full of gaps, a test that fails once in fifty runs. The track whose bad days you can live with is the one you'll stick with.

blocks.title: A track is not a promise of a job

content.text: No track guarantees a job, and demand differs between countries and changes over time. Choose by the work you like, check the local job market as one input, and build the shared basics so you can move if the market does.
How to show your work

Keep your taster projects in one repository with a short note on each: what you built, what you liked and what you didn't. Then put your committed track's projects in their own repositories with clear READMEs. A short post on why you chose your track, with the tasters behind it, shows an interviewer how you make decisions, which matters more than the choice itself.

content.text: Key takeaways

items.text: There is no single best track; the right one is the track whose daily work you can stand on a bad day.
Learn the shared basics first, then try two or three tracks with small taster projects before you commit.
Commit to one roadmap long enough to ship a real project, and grow a little into its neighbors.
Switching later is normal and cheapest to a neighboring track, because your basics move with you.
